list.listitem: The diagnostic evaluation for suspected dementia should include a validated brief cognitive test, laboratory tests focused on reversible causes, functional screening, and ideally an informant questionnaire. C
Brief cognitive tests for dementia appropriate for office practice include the Mini-Mental Status Examination, the Six-Item screener, the AD8, the Time and Change Test, the Mini-Cog, and others. B

Laboratory evaluation should include: complete blood count, thyroid-stimulating hormone, serum calcium and electrolytes, B12, and fasting glucose levels to examine for treatable causes of cognitive decline. Consider serum folate, tests for syphilis, and HIV serology if patient is at risk for those conditions. C
American and Canadian guidelines recommend imaging (preferentially MRI) for most patients as part of the initial evaluation.C

background.definition: Dementia is a syndrome defined by a decline in two or more cognitive domains leading to functional impairment.

list.listitem: Men: 10/1000/year for ages 65 to 69 years, 20/1000/year for ages 70 to 74 years, 25/1000/year for ages 75 to 79 years, 35/1000/year for ages 80 to 84 years, and 65/1000/year for ages 85 years and older.
Women: 8/1000/year for ages 65 to 74 years, 20/1000/year for ages 75 to 79 years, 45/1000/year for ages 80 to 84 years, and 100/1000/year for ages 85 years and older.

The prevalence of dementia rises with age. Interestingly, a study found an overall decrease in dementia from 2000 to 2012. The reasons for this are not fully understood, but thought in part to be due to higher educational achievement.

In the United States, the prevalence is as follows:
65-74 years old: mild cognitive impairment (MCI) 14%, dementia 3% 75-84 years old: MCI 23%, dementia 10% 85 years or older: MCI 30%, dementia 30%
£18 billion/year in the United Kingdom; an average of nearly £25,500 per dementia patient per year (approximately $51,000 US).
A U.S.- based study estimated annual cost of care for a patient with dementia to be between $42,000-$56,000 annually.
Dementia of the Alzheimer's type (DAT).
Vascular dementia (VAD) or multi-infarct dementia (MID).
Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB).
Frontotemporal dementia (FTD).
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD).

The risk of a neurodegenerative disease, including Alzheimer disease, being listed on the death certificate or the risk of being prescribed medications for dementia was about 3 to 5 times higher in Scottish soccer players compared to matched controls.
Dementia of the Alzheimer type: Production and aggregation of amyloid beta peptide, possibly augmented by vascular factors; odds ratio for DAT is 2.8 for one e4 allele and 11.8 for 2 alleles.
Vascular or multi-infarct dementia: Small vessel thrombosis with progressive neuronal loss.
Dementia with Lewy Bodies: Build-up of accumulated alpha-synuclein protein inside neurons.
Frontotemporal dementia: Anterior temporal and frontal lobe atrophy.

Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease: Three subtypes: sporadic, hereditary, and acquired; sporadic most common, appears without risk factors; hereditary associated with family history of CJD; acquired, transmitted by exposure to affected nervous system tissue.
The USPSTF found insufficient evidence for or against routine screening for dementia in healthy older adults.B
Treatment of systolic hypertension may reduce the incidence of dementia, as well as the risk of stroke. C
The USPSTF found insufficient evidence for or against routine screening for dementia in healthy older adults.
If screening is chosen, options include the Delayed Recall Test, the Time and Change Test, Palmer's 3-step procedure, the Mini-Mental Status Examination or the Mini-Cog. See .
Brief instruments screening for cognitive impairment can identify dementia; however evidence is lacking that screening can improve clinical outcomes.

The Rowland Universal Dementia Assessment Scale (RUDAS) is a cognitive assessment tool for the assessment of dementia. It has a LR+ of 5.5 and a LR− of 0.28 for the diagnosis of dementia and is less affected by language and educational attainment than the MMSE.

Among 2,690 primary care patients (aged 70-78 years) a decline in the Visual Association Test (VAT) plus a 2-point decline in the MMSE was associated with a higher predictive value in identifying those at elevated risk for dementia over a 2-year period of time (OR = 9.55) compared to the use of the MMSE alone (OR = 3.55).

A 2020 Lancet Commision identified 12 key modifiable risk factors for dementia, contributing to an estimated 40% of dementias worldwide. Addressing these risk factors could reduce risk for dementia: Treat hypertension to a goal of less than 130 systolic starting in midlife Stop smoking. Minimize diabetes. Prevent head injury. Reduce air pollution. Reduce midlife obesity. Maintain frequent exercise. Reduce occurence of depression. Avoid excessive alcohol consumption. Treat hearing impairment. Maintain frequent social contact. Attain high level of education.

The 5th Canadian Consensus Conference on Dementia identified 8 areas for primary and secondary prevention of dementia: Nutrition: a Mediterranean diet, low in saturated fats and high in fruits and vegetables Regular exercise of at least moderate intensity. Avoid and treat hearing loss. Optimize sleep Maintain cognitive stimulation. Poverty reduction and support for educational attainment Manage frailty Reduce polypharmacy.

In a prospective cohort study, higher Mediterranean-type diet adherence and higher physical activity were independently associated with reduced risk for Alzheimer disease (absolute risk reduction = 7%; HR 0.65; 95% CI, 0.44-0.96).

Severe hypoglycemic episodes increase the risk of dementia for patients with type 2 diabetes; attributable risk of dementia for patients with 1 or more episodes compared with those with no episodes was 2.39% per year.

In a systematic review that included 46 studies and 61,000 patients, the use of anticholinergic medications in the elderly was associated with cognitive and physical decline. In this same study they used a tool called the anticholinergice burden scale to identify eligible medications.
There is good evidence from RCTs that statins given in late life to individuals at risk of vascular disease have no effect in preventing AD or dementia.
Estrogens with or without progestins should be avoided if taken solely to reduce dementia risk.
In the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) 1000 mg calcium plus 400 IU vitamin D once daily were no better than placebo in preventing cognitive decline in women older than 65 years.
Computerized cognitive training to improve cognition in healthy elders is of uncertain benefit.

Differential.Differential_Features: Progressive worsening of memory/cognition, altered behavior patterns, family history
Stepwise progression, focal neurologic findings, dysexecutive syndrome
Visual hallucinations and fluctuations in disease course
Younger onset age, prominent behavior changes, language impairment
Classic triad of cognitive impairment, gait abnormality and urinary incontinence
Cognitive decline in the absence of functional impairment
Acute onset of fluctuating cognition with prominent inattention and consciousness
Particularly those on the BEERS list including anticholinergics, barbituates, benzodiazepines.

list.listitem: The DSM-V makes a distinction between Major Neurocognitive Disorders (which includes all types of dementia) and Mild Neurcognitive Disorder (which is equivalent to Mild Cognitive Impairment). See .
National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) criteria are 43% sensitive and 95% specific for VAD.
Hachinski Ischemic Score is 89% sensitive and 89% specific for VAD or MID.
Clinical criteria function poorly to differentiate LBD from DAT, but Consortium for Dementia with Lewy Bodies criteria are most widely used (sensitivity 22%, specificity 100%).

Early loss of personal awareness, early loss of social awareness, hyperorality, and stereotyped, perseverative behavior were somewhat sensitive (63%-73%) and highly specific (97%-100%) for differentiating DAT from FTD.
Poser criteria appear to have a sensitivity of 97% and a specificity of 98% for dementia due to CJD.
Newly proposed criteria based primarily on amyloid and tau deposition rather than clinical criteria fail to accurately classify most patients with dementia.

History should focus on the cadence of impairment (steady progression versus stepwise worsening of symptoms), relation to vascular events (i.e., stroke), presence of alcohol/substance abuse, presence of mood disorders, and risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, smoking history, family history of dementia, history of head trauma, educational level).

Take a separate history from a caregiver or family member regarding time course, behavioral changes, and functional impairment (memory, cognition, speech). Behavioral changes may be noted only by caregivers, not the patient.

Ask the caregiver or family members about activities of daily living and higher function activities likely to be impaired in early dementia, such as driving, management of financial affairs, attention to hobbies, the ability to learn new skills, and other higher level executive functions.
Physical examination: signs of stroke, abnormal neurologic findings (hyperreflexia, Babinski sign, gait apraxia, pseudobulbar palsy).
Having a memory complaint is of limited value in predicting the onset of DAT within 3 years. However, presence of memory complaint plus evidence of global cognitive impairment is more accurate.
Consider Lewy body dementia in patients with parkinsonism or a history of Parkinson's disease and/or prominent visual hallucinations.
Consider Creutzfeldt-Jacob disease in patients with rapidly progressive dementia, especially in those who are younger or have risk factors for CJD.

In a well-educated cohort of elders with no baseline cognitive impairment, self-reported memory concerns were associated with an increased risk of cognitive impairment. Of those with memory complaints, 25% showed objective cognitive impairment, with approximately 50% of these going on to develop dementia after 9 to 11 years.

Laboratory evaluation should include: complete blood count, thyroid-stimulating hormone, serum calcium and electrolytes, B12, and fasting glucose levels to examine for treatable causes of cognitive decline. Consider serum folate, tests for syphilis, and HIV serology if patient is at risk for those conditions.

Canadian and Italian guidelines recommend neuroimaging for most patients with cognitive complaints including: onset of cognitive signs/symptoms in the past 2 years; unexpected/unexplained cognitive or functional decline in a patient with known dementia, recent head trauma, unexplained nervous system symptoms, history of cancer, bleeding disorder, history of urinary incontinence or gait disorder, new localizing signs, unusual or atypical cognitive symptoms or presentation. MRI is preferred over CT as it is more sensitive to for vascular lesions.

Among 1721 patients aged 65 to 80 without evidence of dementia at baseline and followed for 10 years, baseline MRI findings of white matter lesion volume, brain volume, hipocampal volume were not predictive of the subsequent development of dementia.
American Academy of Neurology guidelines recommend neuroimaging with CT or MRI as part of the initial evaluation of patients with dementia.
CSF beta-amyloid and CSF p-tau are useful in differentiating DAT from FTD, but require lumbar puncture and are not routinely recommended.
The plasma tau217 blood test was evaluated in 3 cohorts with a approximately 1200 participants. THe AUC was between 0.89 and 0.96. Other similar bioimarkers are being evaluated.
Although not recommended for routine diagnosis of dementia, functional scanning such as PET can aid in differentiating DAT from FTD and in identifying questionable early cases of DAT.

Canadian guidelines recommend that genetic testing for the APOE genotype may be offered to the following individuals at increased risk: first-degree relatives of an affected person with the mutation, first cousins of an affected person if the common ancestor died before the average family age of dementia onset, and nieces and nephews of an affected person whose parent died before the average family age of dementia onset.

The presence of 3 biomarkers at baseline is associated with an increased risk of progression to MCI or dementia among patients with a subjective complaint of memory loss (amyloid odds ratio [OR] 5.89; 95% CI 2.33 - 14.90; phosphorylate tau OR 3.99; 2.34 - 6.85; total tau OR 2.26; 1.14 - 4.48)

In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 studies with 7.1 million observations, military veterans who experience TBI were more likely to develop all-cause and vascular dementia (pooled HR 1.95), but not Alzheimer’s dementia.

Brief cognitive tests for dementia appropriate for office practice include the Mini-Mental Status Examination, the 6-item screener, the AD8, the Time and Change Test, the Mini-Cog, and others. See for a summary of their accuracy.
The Mini-Cog in particular has been well validated in the primary care setting, is easy to administer, and has adequate accuracy as an initial tool for the evaluation of suspected dementia.
A self-administered cognitive test, TYM (test your memory) is another screening option for Alzheimer's disease. Practitioners should become familiar with one screening tool and use it consistently.
A version of the MOntreal Cognitive Assessment (MOCA) has been validated in the hearing impaired.
The probability of developing dementia in 20 years can be estimated by a validated clinical decision rule.
See for a suggested approach to evaluation of the patient with suspected dementia.

cell.label: Dementia suspected: perform history (timing, risk factors, family history, head trauma, education) and interview caregiver. Perform physical exam (signs of previous stroke, hyperreflexia, Babinski signs, gait apraxia, pseudobulbar palsy).
Administer brief cognitive test (e.g., Mini-Mental State Examination,Time and Change). Do history, physical, and cognitive test suggest dementia?
Lab evaluation: CBC, TSH, electrolytes, serum calcium, fasting glucose, B12. Abnormal?

Age <60, rapid decline over 1-2 months, duration of dementia <2 years, recent head trauma, unexplained neurologic symptoms, history of cancer, use of anticoagulants or bleeding disorder, history of urinary incontinence and gait disorder, new localizing signs, atypical presentation, or new gait disorder?

Alzheimer's dementia likely. Consider Lewy body dementia if prominent visual hallucinations and parkinsonian signs. Consider CJD and CSF 14-2-2 antigen testing if rapid decline with risk factors for CJD.
Evaluate and treat abnormal findings. Symptoms resolve?
Evaluate/treat the depression, source of delirium. Symptoms resolve?
